item.title: California Thieves Carried Out String of Train Heists, Prosecutors Say
item.description:
The train robberies outlined in the 49-page indictment read like a Hollywood treatment for a Wild West-meets-the-A.I.-age heist movie.

Over more than two years, prosecutors say, a crew of 14 people carried out a series of freight train heists in Southern California, boarding the slow-moving trains in early-morning darkness. After sawing their way into boxcars stuffed with sneakers and electronics, they forced the trains to a stop, filled waiting getaway vans with the goods and fled to stash houses, according to the grand jury indictment unsealed on Thursday.

The thieves were as meticulous in documenting their exploits as they were in planning them, according to the indictment, which includes images from a video showing one of the accused using a circular saw to cut the lock of a train car, sparks flying. In some instances, those charged had posted videos of their crimes to social media, officials said.

The group called themselves the “Los Trenes” — Spanish for “The Trains,” according to prosecutors. In an Instagram chat described in the indictment, the crew members shared A.I.-generated images of black-clad men in black BMWs driving alongside a train as their accomplices unload boxes of Nike shoes.

Over more than two years, prosecutors say, their take was staggering: more than $22 million worth of Nike, Hoka and Crocs shoes, as well as electronics and power tools. Altogether, the crew plundered more than three dozen train cars, officials said.

Law enforcement officers on Thursday fanned out across Southern California to make arrests.

The charges followed a 14-month task force investigation, named Operation CoolKicks, that involved numerous agencies, including the Los Angeles Police Department, the Department of Justice, the Los Angeles District Attorney’s Office, Homeland Security Investigations and the Union Pacific Railroad police.

Jim McDonnell, chief of the Los Angeles Police Department, said at a news conference on Thursday that the indictment “marks the largest property crime bust in L.A.P.D. and railroad history.”

“This is much more than a modern-day train robbery,” he said. “It was a highly coordinated operation that disrupted our nation’s supply chain.”

The indictment charged 14 men with 17 felony counts related to the heists, and they face decades in prison if convicted, according to the Justice Department. It was unclear whether any of the men charged had legal representation.

Southern California is a hub for America’s supply chain, with goods arriving by sea at two ports, Los Angeles and Long Beach, where they are then loaded onto trains bound for warehouses around the country. In recent years, trains, especially in the Los Angeles area, have been targeted by thieves with greater frequency, and law enforcement has devoted more resources to countering the crimes.

“The scale of the theft is staggering,” said Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney in Los Angeles, whose office is prosecuting the case. Mr. Essayli posted a video on X of the man prosecutors say was the crew’s ringleader sawing off a lock on a train car.

“I encourage criminals to film themselves while committing crimes,” Mr. Essayli said at the news conference. “It makes our jobs a lot easier.”

The robbery crew had their own network of stash houses and warehouses across the region, according to the indictment. Once the looted goods were safely stored, they arranged to sell the products to buyers who would then resell them to the public. One company, a sneaker reseller identified only as “Company 1” in the indictment, operated a warehouse in Santa Monica, Calif., and paid more than $1 million over the last two years for stolen Nikes, prosecutors say.

The indictment describes a series of train heists from February of 2024 until this summer. The goods had been on their way to places all around the country, including Indiana, Texas, Kansas and Pennsylvania.

Each heist involved several men, with some jumping onboard the moving freight trains, which were as much as three miles long. Other members of the crew, using rented vans and trucks, positioned themselves ahead of the train’s route at an agreed-upon, often remote and isolated, location. Once the train reached that spot, one of the men on board would cut the hose supplying air to the brakes, “forcing the trains to come to an emergency stop,” prosecutors wrote.

Once the getaway vehicles were stuffed with sneakers or tools or electronics, the goods would be stored at stash houses while the men arranged transactions with resellers.

Well before the arrests this week, the crew had hints that law enforcement officers were on their tail.

According to the indictment, an unnamed co-conspirator sent a text to one of the defendants saying he had been arrested for receiving stolen property. He wrote that he “could have easily thru your name under the bus.”

The last robbery detailed in the indictment was on Aug. 6. The man prosecutors say was the leader of the operation boarded a train and discovered an especially valuable stash of unreleased Nike Air Jordan “Space Jam” sneakers.

Prosecutors say he texted a photograph to the group chat. “No way,” one of the members replied. “Sheeeesh,” wrote another.

item.title: Justice Department Gives Up on Alaska Senate Lawsuit
item.description:
The Trump administration is giving up its bid to block the certification of results in Alaska’s Senate race, abandoning a legal maneuver that threatened to prevent Senator-elect Mary Peltola, a Democrat, from taking office.

The Justice Department asked a federal court to declare its lawsuit against Alaska moot on Thursday, two days after The Associated Press called the competitive race for Ms. Peltola.

Democrats helped recruit a second candidate with a name similar to that of the Republican incumbent, Senator Dan S. Sullivan, The New York Times reported. On President Trump’s order, the Justice Department had argued even before Election Day, and before The Times’s report, that Alaska should not certify a narrow victory for Ms. Peltola until it could be determined that her win was not due to voter confusion.

But critics called the move legally meritless, and lawyers for the state of Alaska, where Republicans control the governorship and the Legislature, sought to have the case dismissed.

Ms. Peltola ended up winning by more than four percentage points, a wide enough margin that Mr. Sullivan would still have lost even if every ballot cast for the lesser-known candidate had gone to him.

In a court filing on Thursday, the Justice Department maintained that its initial bid had merit, but it conceded that it would be impossible for its lawyers to interrogate voters about their reasoning now that ballots had been de-identified. Lawyers for the Justice Department “reluctantly” acknowledged that “there no longer exists any means” to figure out whether voters for the potential spoiler, Dan J. Sullivan, meant to pick the incumbent senator instead, and therefore no way to vindicate its claims.

A judge denied the Trump administration’s request to segregate ballots cast for Dan J. Sullivan ahead of the election, but the Justice Department appealed.

The judge could still rule on the merits of the case, even though the Justice Department argues the point is moot.

In October, the Justice Department announced it was investigating Democrats who recruited a decoy Alaska Senate candidate over potential illegal activity. Thursday’s filings did not address the status of that inquiry, which prosecutors acknowledged might never yield criminal charges.

The Justice Department sent letters to 20 Democrats informing them that they might be targets or asking them to preserve their records, and issued hundreds of subpoenas, according to a person familiar with the investigation who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation.

Ms. Peltola has claimed she was unaware of the plan to recruit a spoiler.

Mr. Sullivan’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In a statement responding to Thursday’s filing, Ms. Peltola said that “voters sent a very clear message about the direction they want our state to go in” and added that she was eager to “get to work on behalf of all Alaskans.”

“For Alaskans, there is only one direction: forward,” she said.

Kellen Browning contributed reporting from Anchorage and Devlin Barrett from Washington.

item.title: New Ph.D. Enrollment in the Sciences Dropped 10 Percent Under Trump
item.description:
The number of new Ph.D. students studying science, engineering, health, mathematics and computer science at major research institutions in the United States fell substantially during the first year of President Trump’s second term, according to a new federal survey.

The decline, about as steep as what occurred during the Covid-19 pandemic, was largely — but not entirely — driven by a drop in international students. It indicates that schools are pulling back on research in a range of fields amid the turbulence in higher education.

First-time doctoral students at 187 top research schools

Source: National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics

According to an analysis of the survey data by The New York Times, the overall number of new full-time doctoral students in the surveyed fields at the nation’s 187 top research schools fell by about 5,100 in 2025. That number represented a decline of 11 percent from the prior school year. A similar trend held across the survey’s broader set of schools, which saw a decline of 10 percent.

Plummeting enrollment among international students accounted for nearly three-quarters of the drop at the top research schools, a sign that those students may have been dissuaded from studying in the United States by the Trump administration’s crackdown on immigrants and efforts to limit visa stays.

A White House report released over the summer, which committed to initiating a “new golden age” of American science, described an “overreliance” on international talent as an issue of national security. “The United States has funded large cohorts of foreign students and tolerated technology transfer abroad under lax security standards,” the report read. “This reliance on foreign talent sidelines American students, a deep domestic talent pool that remains undersupported by its own government.”

But according to the survey data, the number of U.S. citizens and permanent residents enrolling in full-time doctoral programs also dropped. At top research schools, 1,450 fewer of these students enrolled in 2025 than in the previous year.

Funds that support doctoral research have been disrupted as the federal government cut or threatened grant money, agencies lost staff and the Trump administration shifted to new priorities.

The total number of full-time doctoral students remained essentially flat. But the declines are the first time that new enrollments have fallen since 2020, when they dropped due to pandemic restrictions before rising again in 2021 as those restrictions eased.

The data does not capture any changes this school year, but information collected from a group of major research schools shows even steeper declines among doctoral enrollments this fall.

“Graduate students are both today’s and tomorrow’s scientific work force, and a sustained decline in doctoral enrollments could affect research capacity for years to come,” said Travis York, a director at the American Association for the Advancement of Science. “It’s the people entering doctoral programs today that will lead discoveries in biotechnology, computing, energy, engineering, A.I. and other fields over the next decade.”

The new figures come from an annual survey by the National Science Foundation of institutions across the United States that offer graduate degrees in science, engineering or health programs. Known as the Survey of Graduate Students and Postdoctorates in Science and Engineering, the findings offer broad insight into enrollment and completion trends for master’s and Ph.D. students in STEM fields.

In 2025, 93 percent of the 635 surveyed institutions responded, including all 187 classified as schools with the highest levels of research spending and Ph.D. production, also known as R1 institutions.

Of those elite research institutions, 132 enrolled fewer new doctoral students in the surveyed fields in 2025 than in 2024.

The Times analyzed trends at these schools, and found that new, full-time Ph.D. enrollments in engineering programs fell by 14 percent. In science and health fields, the collective drop was nearly 11 percent, while mathematics and computer science enrollments together fell by 8 percent.

A previous Times analysis of new Ph.D. enrollments at 27 major research universities in the country found similar trends.

Some fields, like biology and biomedical programs, civil engineering and medical research, were hit especially hard. But no field saw an increase in incoming Ph.D. students.

Source: National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics

In addition to physical and life sciences, such as chemistry and biology, the federal survey also includes data on social sciences like anthropology, economics and sociology. New enrollments in those fields declined by about 10 percent.

The survey’s findings are in line with other data showing a substantial decline in international students choosing to pursue degrees in the United States. New enrollments by doctoral students on temporary visas fell by almost 17 percent at major research universities in the N.S.F. survey, more than twice the rate of declines among citizens and permanent residents.

The drop in the number of foreign students embarking on master’s degrees was even larger, with enrollments declining 28 percent at major research universities. The number of U.S. citizens and permanent residents entering those programs increased by 9 percent.

While most universities saw a decrease in new graduate enrollments, a handful saw a significant rise.

The University of Texas at Austin had one of the largest increases of incoming Ph.D. students, both domestic and international, among all R1 universities. Its mathematics and computer science programs saw enrollment rise from 56 students in 2024 to 94 in 2025. University administrators credited the increase to a dedicated strategy to support growth in federal research funding.

While many universities have seen funding disruptions under the Trump administration and individual researchers have lost grants, some schools have seen increases, often in areas linked to government priorities.

U.T. Austin already had a research portfolio “that really aligns with federal priorities,” said Fernanda Leite, the university’s vice president for research. That includes artificial intelligence, energy, quantum computing and material sciences.

David Vanden Bout, dean of the college of natural sciences at U.T. Austin, said that the university also made a choice not to cut back on Ph.D. admissions despite funding uncertainties and visa restrictions.

“There has been a hope that that would actually give us a competitive advantage,” he said. “Because as other schools cut back on their admissions, we were going to get a greater lion’s share of the really top students.”

Dr. York noted that, while the survey provides a broad snapshot of graduate enrollment trends across the nation, many questions remain, including how the declines impacted students of different socioeconomic backgrounds and where prospective Ph.D. students went instead. He also emphasized that this data only reflects the first year of the second Trump administration.

As more data comes out, he said, it will “illuminate how funding or immigration uncertainties are currently influencing university and student decision making.”

item.title: These Underdogs Were Just Elected. No One Is More Surprised Than They Are.
item.description:
Nathan Miller was in his barn milking a cow when he found out he might actually win the election.

His wife’s phone pinged with every new batch of results, and what had started as a lark for the 51-year-old dairy farmer began to feel very real.

Mr. Miller, a left-leaning political independent who often supports the Green Party in national races, had signed up to run for county assessor in conservative northwest Arkansas mostly to make a point. He was tired of seeing Republican politicians go unopposed.

“That doesn’t seem like any kind of democracy,” said Mr. Miller, who wears his hair long, keeps his beard bushy and used to play mandolin in a bluegrass punk band called Cletus Got Shot.

Mr. Miller, who registered as a Democrat before declaring his candidacy, was not expecting to beat the Republican incumbent, and he did not try very hard. He didn’t campaign or seek donations. He spent $225 of his own money on a few signs and said he disclosed the expenditure “for legal purposes” in a TikTok video, posted under the username This Old Hillbilly.

But as dusk settled over Washington County on Election Day and Mr. Miller coaxed milk from Iris, one of his 13 cows, it became clear that he would win — and that his life was about to change.

Democrats across the country were having similar experiences. By week’s end, their party had scored splashy, headline-grabbing victories from coast to coast. But another measure of the landslide’s magnitude emerged down ballot, in Democrats’ unlikely successes in state and local races, where they prevailed against eye-popping odds on ruby-red terrain.

Those under-the-radar contests are often less susceptible to national trends, but this year, even some of the longest long shots surfed the blue wave into office.

“People didn’t just go and say ‘no’ at the top of the ticket; they didn’t stop at the Senate,” said Kim Rogers, a Democratic strategist who specializes in state and local elections. “They wanted to make sure Republicans felt this all the way down the ballot.”

Seething over soaring prices and President Trump’s war with Iran, American voters elected Democrats whom most prognosticators had picked to lose. Perhaps no one was more surprised than many of the winners, who now find themselves scrambling to rearrange their lives around new positions, quitting day jobs, strategizing child care and studying up on roles they never thought they would assume.

In Arizona’s Maricopa County, a 19-year-old college sophomore was elected Superior Court clerk, an office that oversees 600 employees and a $65 million budget, despite believing he was running “a sacrificial-lamb race.”

In western Iowa, a former railroad executive withdrew from his race for the State House early because he said he was too sick to serve. In North Texas, a State House candidate suspended her campaign after opponents revealed she had a felony conviction. Both were Democrats who won anyway and say they plan to take office (though the Texas winner’s eligibility is now being weighed by the State Supreme Court).

And in California, a former small town mayor ousted one of the State Assembly’s most powerful Republicans, fueled by a campaign that reported a fund-raising haul of $0.

Many other Democrats made history. Brian Matlock will be the first member of his party elected Arizona mine inspector since 1974, when outrage over the Watergate scandal propelled an earlier crop of Democrats into office. The party had frequently written off the role, often leaving Republicans unopposed.

Mr. Matlock, a mechanical engineer, had no political experience. But he had his wife, who was willing to help him gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot and serve as his campaign manager.

The two crisscrossed the state towing a camper that they slept in after events to save money on hotel costs. Mine inspector is a conservative-coded position, but Mr. Matlock steered clear of partisan issues and focused on miner safety. His outlaw facial hair may have helped, too.

“I have a funny mustache, and they figured I looked the part,” he said.

In Grand County, Colo., the chair of the local Democratic Party, Liz Newsom, said she tried for months to persuade neighbors to challenge the county’s sitting Republicans. She placed an ad in the newspaper listing salaries for the elected positions, hoping to entice candidates.

But there were no takers, Ms. Newsom said, so she decided to run herself. She entered the race for clerk and recorder, the top local elections official, and won by seven percentage points. It was the only countywide race to feature a Democrat. Ms. Newsom is hoping her example will make recruiting easier in 2028.

“Seeing you can win is very helpful for people,” Ms. Newsom said. “Until now, it was like, ‘Why would I do this? I’m just going to get abused for no reason.’”

In a fast-growing suburb east of Dallas, Marcus and Shree Henderson needed hardly any convincing when local Democratic officials encouraged them to run in an area Mr. Trump had won by nearly 30 points in 2024. They just needed to know they could do it the same way they coach volleyball and lead a couples ministry — as a pair.

So Mr. Henderson picked justice of the peace and Ms. Henderson chose commissioner, and they launched a joint campaign that urged people to “Vote Henderson” in a county where no Democrat had won this century. They juggled full-time jobs, he as an insurance underwriter and she as a social worker, door-knocking during lunch breaks. In the end, their races were not even close.

“We’re still shocked,” Ms. Henderson said. “I don’t think it’s all clicked that we’ve won.”

Mr. Miller can relate. He confessed to “getting a bit of the jitters” once he knew he had come out on top. He talked with his wife about “the impostor syndrome crap” that might set in once he takes charge of his 38-person staff, a crew smaller than his flock of sheep but more intimidating.

Yet the more he learned about the county assessor job, the more excited he got. Mr. Miller thinks the property tax system, whose rates the assessor sets, is rife with inequities and could use an overhaul. Then there’s the salary, which, at $155,000, is by far the best paying job he has ever landed.

Mr. Miller describes himself as “a quiet moderate,” a gun owner who believes everyone has the right to “let your freak flag fly,” no matter their race, religion, gender or sexuality. Republicans, especially those in his deep-red state, have been trying to chip away at those personal freedoms, he said, and “people who were not being represented got tired of it and finally stood up.”

Mr. Miller’s nascent political career has not been totally smooth. He took his first lump during the campaign, when he posted a video musing about the prospect of winning: “I might get the job, and heck, I don’t even want it,” he said with a laugh. His opponent latched onto the statement as proof that Mr. Miller was not a serious candidate.

But Mr. Miller said his critics had the wrong idea — it wasn’t that he didn’t want to do the job, it was that he’d be sad to leave full-time farm life behind.

“My wife says I’ve got to watch my filter a bit,” he said.

Not too much, though, because he doesn’t want to become something he’s not: a politician.

“When I think of ‘politician,’ I think of that suit that’s disconnected from their constituents,” Mr. Miller said. “I don’t want to become that politician. I want to stay Nathan.”

Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

item.title: Is There Room for Ron DeSantis in a Post-Trump World? He Seems to Think So.
item.description:
For someone who says he has not yet figured out his political future, Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida has become unusually chatty about it.

He won’t say whether he is going to run for president, but he is already calculating what timing would be best. He was accused of waiting too long to get in when he ran three years ago, but now he thinks getting in too early might be the mistake to avoid this time.

“A lot of people, if they’re smart, they would kind of wait to see how things are developing,” Mr. DeSantis, 48, told The New York Times in a wide-ranging interview on Wednesday. “Because you want to have a message that you know is going to be pertinent for the 2028 election, right?”

He described how a would-be presidential campaign would be different from his 2024 bid; what he learned about himself and managing the news media; and even the weaknesses of a potential Republican rival — although he did not refer to Vice President JD Vance by name.

“V.P.s tend to be derivative,” he said. They are validated by the president who chose them but also stuck at No. 2, often unable to win over many of the president’s detractors.

The question for Mr. DeSantis is whether there is room for him in a post-Trump world. He seems to think so — though he is still figuring out exactly how.

He could start a conservative think tank. He could hit the lucrative speaker circuit. He could run for president again, either in 2028 or 2032.

“What I’m interested in is producing results,” the term-limited governor said. He declined to reveal what he will do once he leaves the job in January.

But he offered a bracing assessment of where the Republican Party is, and should go, in the aftermath of its disastrous midterm election results.

Mr. DeSantis has made an unlikely re-emergence out of that wreckage, sitting for a flurry of interviews to showcase how Florida withstood a national Democratic landslide. His appearances, coming more than two years after he withdrew from the 2024 presidential primary and largely turned his attention to his home state, have renewed chatter about his ambitions.

“I haven’t made any decisions,” Mr. DeSantis said of another presidential run.

He denied a report that he was putting together a campaign team — “That’s just not true,” he said — and argued that assembling a 2028 presidential operation so soon after the midterms would be “very premature.”

He also said he thinks the Republican field is likely to crystallize more slowly than in the past as presidential contenders take time to assess the political landscape — and speculate about the contours of a post-Trump world.

“There’s a lot of questions about, you know, what’s the trajectory of the economy looking like?” he said. “How are the Democrats going to use their power? You know, how are all these things going to kind of shake out?”

“Politics is contextual,” he added.

“The terrain that we’re going to be on as a party is going to change some. It can definitely get better. It could also erode in some respects.”

Mr. DeSantis was uncertain about whether the next presidential election would be good for his party — not because of the drubbing Republicans received in the midterms, but because the presidency has rarely changed hands within the same party.

The governor’s name has come up several times as a potential cabinet pick, including for defense secretary. Mr. DeSantis denied having talked to President Trump about any such position. He said he does not expect a Democratic Senate to confirm any of the president’s nominees.

Mr. DeSantis, a former Navy lawyer, has also been said to be interested in the Supreme Court. He scoffed at the idea.

“I’m an executive. I lead, I get ahead of things,” he said.

“To say that you’re going to end up a potted plant on the Supreme Court and just kind of sit there,” he added, “and I respect the justices, and people like Clarence Thomas have been heroes of mine for many years, but it just — it’s totally contrary to what I’ve demonstrated and brought to the table.”

He predicted that Democrats would likely still control the House and Senate when the next president takes office in 2029, which could complicate governing should a Republican succeed Mr. Trump.

But Democrats could “overreach” once they control both chambers of Congress in January, he said, and that could help frame the 2028 election. Democrats would get in trouble, he said, if they try “eliminating the Electoral College, packing the Supreme Court, making D.C. a state, making Puerto Rico a state.”

“That’s not what voters have been asking for,” he said.

Mr. DeSantis’s fundamental argument has not changed much from when he ran for president the first time. The question, as he put it, is whether the political context has.

He is still a conservative warrior in the nation’s third most-populous state with a policy record that even his critics characterize as hugely consequential to Florida. He put the state on the forefront of right-wing policy on everything from school vouchers to vaccine exemptions to immigration enforcement.

“We have so many people that run for office, and they spout platitudes, they get in, and don’t deliver,” he said in his most extensive interview with The Times since he became governor. “I never made promises I couldn’t keep. If I told you I was going to do it, I delivered. I had a plan as to how I was going to do it. I understood the levers of power. I understood where the pressure points were.”

When Mr. DeSantis entered the presidential primary in 2023, he was seen as the Republican with the best chance to dethrone Mr. Trump. He could pursue Trumpism, his supporters argued, without Mr. Trump’s drama.

But Mr. Trump cast him as weak and a traitor to the MAGA movement. Indictments against Mr. Trump in four criminal cases rallied the party around him.

“When he kept getting indicted, it just blotted out the sun,” Mr. DeSantis said.

Mr. DeSantis shunned the national news media in the presidential campaign — something he now says he would approach differently.

“A presidential campaign is so much about the earned media, the free media, and you’ve just got to be out there,” he said. “I think my view going into it was, ‘Look, my record speaks for itself. The media is going to not give me a fair shake; I’m not going to worry about it.’ And I don’t think that was the right way to do it.”

Since 2024, Mr. DeSantis has repaired his relationship with Mr. Trump. It has helped to live in the same state, where the two chief executives have occasionally played golf together, he said.

“We have a great rapport on a lot of things,” he said.

Underlying that approach may be his adamant belief that some form of Trumpism is here to stay, at least through the next presidential election. His party’s next nominee, Mr. DeSantis said, must explain how he or she will “build off” Mr. Trump’s successes. Nominating a “never Trumper,” he said, “is not going to happen.”

“I mean, like, it’s just ridiculous when people start talking in those terms,” he said. “He’s the dominant figure in the party to this day. His involvement, if he gets involved, will be tremendously important.”

But a governor famous for fighting culture wars also said there will be new issues for voters to care about. In the waning days of the midterm campaign, he criticized Republicans for running ads on transgender rights, an issue he fought hard on just a few years ago.

“The problem,” he said, “is that’s not what the voters were voting on in this election.”

Mr. DeSantis spent months warning that the midterms might be difficult for Republicans. In an interview with the podcaster Stephen A. Smith released the day before Election Day, he chided others in his party for not acknowledging how the Iran war had led to higher gas prices.

“If you can’t admit that to voters, then you’re gaslighting them, and they’re not going to listen to you on other things,” Mr. DeSantis said on the podcast.

That interview, which has garnered more than 700,000 views on YouTube, suggested that Mr. DeSantis had been thinking through — if not outright preparing — for the possibility of vast Republican losses, including perhaps in Florida.

Florida stayed red, but barely. Representative Byron Donalds won the governor’s race by about one percentage point. Republicans lost their supermajorities in the state’s House and Senate. Four congressional districts that Republican state lawmakers had redrawn to favor their party at Mr. DeSantis’s insistence remained in Democratic hands.

One reality that Mr. DeSantis will have to confront as he ponders his next step is this: A lot of people in his own party don’t like him. And sometimes, he doesn’t like them back.

The animus for him within the Trump administration stemmed partly from his fractured relationship with Susie Wiles, the recently departed White House chief of staff. Ms. Wiles helped Mr. DeSantis become governor in 2018 before he banished her from his inner circle, privately questioning her loyalty and cutting her out of in-state politics. When asked about her in the interview, he declined to pass judgment on her White House tenure, saying he would leave that to others.

The governor has complicated relationships in his own state, too.

He remains Florida’s most popular Republican and was a formidable fund-raiser and campaigner in the 2022 midterms, when he won re-election by 19 points. This year, he took credit for helping pass a ballot measure that will significantly cut property taxes on homeowners’ primary residences. Doing so drew Republicans to the polls who otherwise might have not voted, he said.

Still, he had returned to Florida after his loss in the presidential race with his stature diminished. Some Republican state lawmakers who had previously bent to his will began to challenge him. Some of those same Republicans grumbled privately throughout the campaign this year that Mr. DeSantis was doing little to help them.

Mr. DeSantis also did not back Mr. Donalds or anyone else in the primary to succeed him.

He pleaded guilty to one of the accusations — and was unapologetic about it.

“The one thing that would be fair to say — because it is accurate — is that I did not help the Florida House of Representatives,” he said. “And basically, it was because they fought me for two years, even though they swept in on my coattails.”

Republicans lost 16 seats in the State House.

As he considers the future, Mr. DeSantis said he intends to keep his focus on his last remaining weeks as governor. He met privately on Monday with Mr. Donalds and told him about his first order of business come January.

“I said, ‘Byron, I’m going to be on the platform with you when you get sworn in, so just make sure you give a short speech, because by about two or three o’clock, I’m going to be on the first tee,’” Mr. DeSantis said, “‘and I don’t want to be late for that tee time.’”

item.title: 2 Earthquakes Rattle California
item.description:
A pair of earthquakes shook parts of California overnight Thursday, striking near the state’s central coast and Los Angeles a few hours apart.

The first quake, a magnitude-5.0 tremor, occurred around 10:50 p.m. Pacific time near Pinnacles, around 100 miles southeast of San Francisco, according to the United States Geological Survey. People reported feeling the quake as far north as Sacramento and as far south as San Diego, according to the agency’s data.

The agency initially recorded the quake’s magnitude as 5.4, but that figure was later revised down to 5.0 — a moderate tremor that can shake houses, rattle windows and cause minor to moderate damage near the epicenter.

The second quake, of magnitude 4.2, occurred around 3:25 a.m. in Los Angeles County, near Commerce, less than 10 miles from downtown Los Angeles, according to the U.S.G.S.

That quake triggered a response from the Los Angeles Fire Department, which went into “earthquake mode,” the department said in a statement. Staff from each of the department’s more than 100 stations looked for critical infrastructure damage and other issues, the department said.

Early Friday morning, the department said it had completed its check and that no significant infrastructure damage or injuries were recorded within the city of Los Angeles.

The U.S.G.S. said that there was a roughly 30 percent chance that an aftershock of magnitude 3 or greater would hit the area in the coming week.

item.title: Lethal Injection Took an Hour as Texas Executioners Hunted for a Vein
item.description:
An execution by lethal injection in Texas on Thursday took more than an hour as prison workers struggled to find a prisoner’s vein, according to an Associated Press reporter who witnessed the death.

The man who was executed, Reinaldo Dennes, was sentenced to death in the 1996 killing of a diamond broker.

Mr. Dennes was strapped to a gurney around 6 p.m., said the reporter who witnessed the procedure, Michael Graczyk. But it seemed to take longer than usual for the prison staff to find a suitable vein, and the execution team ultimately inserted needles in the prisoner’s left foot and in the left side of his neck, he said.

Mr. Dennes, 70, moaned for several minutes before he began to snore, the reporter added.

Another witness, the Rev. Jeff Hood, a spiritual adviser to death row inmates, also said that the execution took about an hour. He added that his hand was on Mr. Dennes’s shoulder while the prisoner yelled in pain.

“Every jolt of that body came up through my arm,” Mr. Hood said in a news release shared by his nonprofit organization, the Execution Intervention Project, which opposes capital punishment.

“I have stood beside 13 lethal injections,” he added. “A man is supposed to lose consciousness fast.”

According to an execution notice from the Texas Department of Criminal Justice, Mr. Dennes was pronounced dead at 7:08 p.m. His prepared final statement said that he wanted his family to know that he had been “extremely blessed these thirty years,” adding that he hoped that they would “get to know this great gift and great grace of God the father.”

A department spokeswoman did not immediately respond to questions about why the execution took more than an hour.

Lethal injections came under intense scrutiny after Tennessee botched two of its three executions this year, mostly recently in the case of Christa Pike. Tennessee has paused executions as an independent review is conducted into the September execution attempt, which Ms. Pike survived despite two injections of a lethal drug.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

Jesus Jiménez contributed reporting.

item.title: Watchdog Officials Considered Investigating Trump’s Memecoin, Then Punted
item.description:
On Sunday, President Trump will for the third time be hosting a gala to promote the digital token he launched just before he returned to office.

As with the two previous events, it will allow the top buyers of his token, called a memecoin, to have face time with a president who has showered the crypto industry with favors.

But there was a moment when the fate of his memecoin could have turned out very differently.

Soon after the coin’s debut in early 2025, career officials at a federal watchdog agency opened an investigation into possible fraud. Then they quickly backed off, convinced that the agency would never approve the subpoenas or other investigative steps needed to dig into the allegations. The inquiry by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which has not been previously reported, was described by three former agency officials with direct knowledge of it who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of repercussions.

The investigation did not get far enough along to determine whether any wrongdoing had transpired. But the decision not to pursue the inquiry helped clear the way for Mr. Trump to enrich himself through token sales.

He collected at least $636 million last year in transaction and licensing fees, according to his financial disclosures. Nearly a million buyers of his memecoins lost a total of $3.81 billion through the end of June, according to Nansen, a cryptocurrency analytics firm.

The gala at the Trump National Golf Club in Northern Virginia — billed as “the most exclusive dinner in the world” — follows closely on an election that polls indicate turned in part on the issue of government corruption.

Democratic members of Congress have said the event is another attempt by Mr. Trump to monetize the presidency. The gathering explicitly allows supporters to purchase access and funnel money to a sitting president. At the first memecoin dinner, held in May 2025 at the same club, protesters chanted “shame, shame” along the road as the attendees arrived.

Davis Ingle, a White House spokesman, said, “The president’s attendance at a privately organized event does not make it a White House event or government function.”

The promotional efforts have brought diminishing returns for Mr. Trump. The coin’s price spiked temporarily to $16.25 from $9.30 after the first event. It jumped to $4.37 from $2.87 after the second event, a luncheon at Mar-a-Lago, was announced.

Not so this time. The coin is now trading at about a dollar, lower than before the midterm election and down from a peak of $75 in January 2025. Overall, it appears to have become progressively cheaper for coin owners to win invitations to the events and to the more intimate receptions with the president.

For every coin they have purchased, buyers receive a point on a public leaderboard. The longer they hold the tokens, the more points they accrue. The top 185 are invited to the event and the top 29 to a “V.I.P. reception” with Mr. Trump.

The short-lived C.F.T.C. inquiry is the first known federal investigation that targeted a business that directly benefited Mr. Trump since his return to office. The C.F.T.C. is charged with overseeing cryptocurrency and prediction markets, two business sectors in which the Trump family is deeply invested.

A spokeswoman declined to comment on how the agency handled the investigation into the Trump coin.

Agency officials opened the inquiry amid a spate of media reports that some early buyers had profited hugely in the memecoin’s first 48 hours of trading, during which its value peaked. For example, five traders who made huge buys in the first five minutes cleared more than $44 million in profits, according to an analysis by Nansen for The New York Times. The agency also received at least one outside complaint, former officials said.

Only 20 percent of the coins were initially for sale; the Trump Organization and its partner, the entrepreneur Bill Zanker, owned the other 80 percent. Those coins were locked up according to a staggered three-year schedule to reassure buyers that the backers of the coin would not suddenly cash out and rob it of its value — a practice sometimes called a “rug pull.”

Even if Mr. Trump and other backers were barred from selling his coins, though, C.F.T.C. officials were concerned about possible insider trading or other abuses.

The inquiry was assigned to Dan Ullman, an enforcement division lawyer and 16-year veteran of the agency who specialized in cryptocurrency cases. Mr. Ullman, who left the C.F.T.C. in late 2025, declined to comment on the inquiry.

Agency lawyers have the authority to open investigations, but they need the commission’s approval to issue subpoenas, which would have been necessary for identifying suspicious traders. While the memecoin trades are recorded on a public blockchain, many of the buyers are anonymous.

At that time, the board had four commissioners, including two Democrats. But three of them were on their way out, either by choice or because their terms were expiring.

That left Caroline D. Pham, a Republican commissioner whom Mr. Trump had elevated as the agency’s new temporary chairman.

In early April 2025, Ms. Pham directed the agency not to seek to charge crypto players with regulatory violations, The Times has previously reported. She pressured enforcement staff to drop existing crypto investigations, The Times reported.

Given all that, agency officials decided that she would never approve subpoenas involving the president’s cryptocurrency, the people with knowledge of the situation said.

Ms. Pham, who left the agency last year to join a crypto firm, did not respond to requests for comment.

The C.F.T.C. had previously brought at least one case charging illegal manipulation of the price of a memecoin during the Biden administration. In 2021, it charged a businessman and an adviser with a “pump and dump” scheme that involved, in part, the popular “Doge” memecoin. (Elon Musk, who promoted but did not create that coin, borrowed the name for his federal cost-cutting initiative.)

The agency said the two men secretly accumulated the coins and artificially drove up their prices by hyping them on social media — all the while lying to the public about their financial interest in them. They then dumped their holdings and cleared more than $2 million in profits.

Both men also faced criminal charges for commodities fraud and money laundering related to the scheme. The businessman died shortly after he was charged. His adviser paid a civil penalty of $145,000.

item.title: As He Leaves Office, Ken Paxton Drops Suits Against Political Opponents
item.description:
Attorney General Ken Paxton, long seen as the tip of the spear for the conservative legal movement in Texas, is no longer in a fighting mood.

Since losing his bid for the U.S. Senate and watching his fellow Republicans lose every statewide race on Election Day, Mr. Paxton has dropped a number of high-profile lawsuits that antagonized his political opponents and appealed to his base.

In recent days, he has abandoned a yearslong lawsuit seeking to shut down a migrant shelter in El Paso and a separate suit aimed at closing a Houston-based immigrant rights group. He dropped a case against the Council on American-Islamic Relations, or CAIR, the nation’s largest Muslim civil rights group, which Gov. Greg Abbott had labeled a terrorist organization.

Mr. Paxton also decided to dismiss a suit against the N.C.A.A. after accusing the sports association of deceptive advertising for labeling competitions as “women’s sports” when they could include transgender athletes.

The cases helped Mr. Paxton burnish his standing among conservatives and fuel his reputation as a no-holds-barred litigator. The decisions to drop them were welcomed by the defendants in each case, and the legal filings lacked any explanation from Mr. Paxton or lawyers from his office.

Mr. Paxton’s office did not respond to requests for comment.

One case, a five-year-old lawsuit accusing Planned Parenthood of committing Medicaid fraud, has not been dropped by Mr. Paxton’s office, but the U.S. Justice Department signaled its intention to intervene. The move suggested there was concern among conservatives that Texas’ incoming Democratic attorney general, Nathan Johnson, would not continue the case.

In a statement, Mr. Johnson said that “irrespective of the likely political motivation behind it, I applaud the termination of these lawsuits,” adding that it was “the first tangible and important result of the election.”

But Mr. Paxton has not thrown in the towel in every instance. His office revived a lawsuit against the city of Houston this week after John Whitmire, its mayor, said the city’s police officers would no longer notify federal immigration agents about unauthorized migrants encountered during routine street stops. The ultimate resolution of that case will most likely not occur until after Mr. Paxton leaves office.

Since the election, lawyers from Mr. Paxton’s office have repeatedly gone to court to ask judges to withdraw lawsuits they had brought.

The timing suggested to many, including the defendants in the cases, that the election of Mr. Johnson, a Democratic governor and enough Democrats to control the Texas House was a central motivation to drop the lawsuits.

“If it goes away in an instant, then what was this about to begin with? If there’s nothing there, then why was this initiated?” said Ruben Garcia, the executive director of the El Paso shelter Annunciation House. “Then this whole thing is political? That’s not the way justice is supposed to work.”

Mr. Garcia was supposed to be deposed by Mr. Paxton’s lawyers last week in the case against Annunciation House, which was first filed in state court in 2024. But rather than move forward with the deposition, the attorney general’s office simply withdrew the lawsuit.

Still, Mr. Garcia said the legal process had done damage to his nonprofit. “They have almost endless resources to go after people,” he said. The suit confused people into thinking the nonprofit had already been closed down, he said, and prospective volunteers worried that getting involved could land them in trouble.

“When someone calls you a smuggler, a trafficker, that your houses of hospitality are stash houses, that’s really severe,” Mr. Garcia said.

Mr. Paxton’s suit accusing the immigrant rights group FIEL Houston was similarly costly, said its executive director, Cesar Espinosa. The attorney general argued that the organization had violated its nonprofit charter by posting about elections and criticizing the Trump administration. The suit had dragged on since 2024, sapping the group’s resources, Mr. Espinosa said.

“We had to move money from other programs to staff time and resources to be able to be all things on deck with this lawsuit,” he said. “It was a very tough last few years.”

The group had not been given advance warning that the suit would be dropped, he said, and no one explained why.

For Edward Ahmed Mitchell, a deputy director at CAIR, Mr. Paxton’s decision to sue his group was made at a time when many Republican elected officials in Texas, including Mr. Abbott, were embracing anti-Muslim rhetoric and actions.

The lawsuit against CAIR was filed in February, in the middle of the Republican Senate primary, which Mr. Paxton won. He dropped the case this week.

Mr. Mitchell said Republicans had used “American Muslims as a political boogeyman” and it failed with voters. “That is a huge turning point,” he said. “Even in Texas, anti-Muslim hate was not enough.”

item.title: Here’s the latest.
item.description:
President Trump is scheduled to hold a news conference on Friday at noon, where he is expected to praise what he sees as his diplomatic accomplishments during a whirlwind trip to Asia this week that included a meeting with the leaders of Russia and China.

Mr. Trump announced the appearance as he returned from what he called a “great and highly consequential trip.” But the meeting did not deliver concrete plans to address global concerns, including the wars in Iran and Ukraine, the dangers of artificial intelligence, or nuclear proliferation. The president said he would discuss trade deals with Thailand, the Philippines and other countries, though no formal agreements have materialized.

Mr. Trump attended summits in the Philippines and China during the four-day trip, and he met with President Vladmir Putin of Russia and President Xi Jinping of China, the first summit of the leaders of those three world powers.

Mr. Trump did not hold a formal news conference, a departure from custom on foreign trips. The White House has sought to cast the trip as a “historic” display of American power on the global stage, although it produced little more than photo-ops for Mr. Trump, who has long had an affinity for both Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin, whom he calls friends.

Mr. Trump returns to a nation on edge, and questions about his administration’s leadership, after a flurry of digital crises, including aviation-system meltdowns and outages at several large banking systems.

While on his trip, the president largely shrugged off the domestic concerns, from the outages to a sustained slide in the stock market. “It’s life,” Mr. Trump said. “When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”

Here’s what else to know:

Contrasting images: The image of Mr. Trump projecting strength with his counterparts from China and Russia contrasted sharply with the changing dynamic back home, where he will soon share power with Democrats. Read more ›

Arms control: President Trump said during a trilateral summit with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin on Thursday that the three of them were “uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on earth.” Yet after the conversation it was clear they had not agreed to return to the detailed arms control talks that were a centerpiece of diplomacy during the Cold War. And on new threats, including artificial intelligence, the three leaders were largely silent. Read more ›

Answering questions: Mr. Trump’s last formal news conference was in July, at the NATO summit in Turkey. Mr. Trump last took questions from reporters in the briefing room before he departed for Asia, during an appearance alongside Dana White, the chief executive of the U.F.C. whom he jokingly offered the press secretary position. The president acknowledged that he was only kidding and wanted to divert from a bad news cycle days after his party absorbed significant losses in the midterm elections.

item.title: L.A. Wants to Clean Up MacArthur Park. Will Fencing It Off Work?
item.description:
Los Angeles has long searched for ways to clean up MacArthur Park, to rid the space of the drug sales and homeless encampments that have made it a blight on the neighborhood and a target for the Trump administration as an example of failed Democratic leadership.

Now it is trying a new approach. The city has committed more than $2 million to erect a fence around the park that is meant to allow officials to exert more oversight over how the park is used.

Construction began on a temporary barrier on Tuesday, with a permanent fence scheduled to be completed next year. Some efforts to improve the park were already underway, including the installation of more lights around the vast 35-acre space, garbage cleanups and the deployment of more street medics and homeless service providers.

Los Angeles police and the Drug Enforcement Administration had already started to crack down on drug dealers who supply the park dwellers. In May, the agencies carried out a major raid that resulted in the arrest of 18 people who the police said were part of a network selling methamphetamine and fentanyl at the park.

Residents and merchants in the community just west of downtown Los Angeles say the recent law enforcement efforts have made a small but noticeable dent in addressing some of the problems, though they say the park remains relatively unsafe, especially at night.

The city’s plans call for the gates to be shut from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. The police will patrol the park to try to clear it out before closing.

MacArthur Park, named for the World War II general, began its life as Westlake Park in the 1880s and was once the crown jewel of the Westlake neighborhood that was home to affluent residents in the early 20th century. Over time, the park deteriorated as the wealthy fled to other areas of the city and investment in the neighborhood declined.

In the 1980s, the neighborhood became a destination for refugees and immigrants fleeing civil wars in Central America.

Today, the community is largely working class and made up of immigrants from Central America. The space features a sports field, a small auditorium, playgrounds, a recreation center and a large lake that at night reflects the downtown skyline looking east.

The park attracted national attention last summer when the Trump administration sent heavily armed Border Patrol agents and members of the National Guard to conduct a military-style sweep. The operation was intended to be a show of force, led by the ousted Border Patrol leader Gregory Bovino, and led to a confrontation between the agents and Mayor Karen Bass, who said the government was just trying to “demonstrate to the nation their bravado.”

Conservatives have also criticized local nonprofit programs that aim to reduce disease and drug deaths by providing clean syringes to users.

The fence initiative, backed by Mayor Bass and Eunisses Hernandez, the councilwoman representing the area, was undertaken by the city’s recreation and parks commission, which approved the $2.3 million project last month. A chain-link fence is being erected now to seal off a construction area for a permanent fence, which will be green and have several pedestrian entry points. The park will remain open during construction.

The plan drew praise from many in the community eager to rid the neighborhood of illicit activity, and criticism from those opposed to closing off a public space.

The president of the city’s cultural heritage organization wrote in a letter to the parks commission that a permanent fence would detract from the park’s historic character.

The cultural commission suggested instead that the city enclose the park with a more temporary barrier as it had done at Echo Park, another enclave that has struggled with many of the same issues at MacArthur Park. That barrier — a chain-link fence — was taken down after two years.

Though the fence around MacArthur Park is built to be permanent, the city plans to review its effectiveness at improving safety after three years.

On Wednesday, men in orange vests and white hard hats were erecting chain-link fencing.

Donnell Edwards, 31, one of the installers, said many of the local residents were happy to see him and his fellow workers. “They’ve been recording,” he said, adding that some had come up to thank him.

Hugo Lopez, 36, who was walking around the park with his wife and 2-year-old son on Wednesday morning, recounted getting mugged at the park one time. He said he was happy to see what he considered decisive action by the authorities.

“You can’t be here at night because people there are people who are really drugged up who can harm you,” Mr. Lopez said.

But others in the area felt the fence would be yet another eyesore, and a futile attempt at solving an intractable social problem.

“Sometimes these things make you laugh,” said Mateo Antonio, 48, as he wrapped up his morning stretch at the soccer field in the park while listening to salsa music. “This problem has nothing to do with a fence.”

People wanting to get in the park during closed hours, he said, would find a way to get in.

Deisy de Leyva, 50, was worried that homeless people who are moved out of the park would wind up outside her beauty salon across the street.

Business, she said, was already slow because of the economy, and the fear of immigration agents was already keeping many of her customers home.

Near the another section of the park, Norm Langer, 81, the owner of Langer’s Delicatessen, is perhaps the most vocal business owner on matters concerning the park. His highly popular eatery has been around since 1947 and is considered a Los Angeles institution.

“I think the fence will do wonders, but the problem still is going to exist,” Mr. Langer said, sharing Ms. de Leyva’s concern that people who need help would simply be displaced.

The hope, he said, was to see the city ensure they went somewhere to get treatment.

item.title: Spying Suspect’s Chip Network Has Ties to Chinese Military Suppliers
item.description:
Alice Huang, the woman at the center of the Nvidia scandal, has extensive ties through her family and associates to China’s defense industry, according to an independent research firm and corporate filings reviewed by The New York Times.

The findings show a web of relationships, most of them indirect, linking Ms. Huang’s family and companies that acquired Nvidia chips to Chinese state-owned defense contractors that supply the People’s Liberation Army.

The nature of those relationships, including the vital question of whether Nvidia chips ended up being used to support Chinese military projects, remains murky. But the revelations, along with an investigation by The Times published on Wednesday, underscore how the Chinese effort to acquire access to the computing power of Nvidia’s chips is intertwined with Beijing’s desire to harness artificial intelligence to bolster its military capabilities.

That outcome has long been feared by U.S. national security officials, given that the technology could help China develop more sophisticated weapons, carry out cyberattacks and integrate A.I. into the battlefield.

A confidential analysis by Strider Technologies, an independent intelligence firm that employs former intelligence officers and experts on China and specializes in corporate intelligence, shows that about $3.6 billion in Chinese government money flowed through companies associated with Ms. Huang’s family or associates. The government money funded technology projects, including data centers that received Nvidia chips.

The New York Times reviewed the Strider findings. Many of the corporate ties revealed by Strider were independently confirmed by The Times.

The Times reported last month that U.S. officials believe Ms. Huang, a Chinese citizen also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese intelligence asset who was providing information to the Ministry of State Security. The Strider Technologies analysis and the review of corporate filings by The Times show that she; her sister, Huang Yu; and an investor named Kang Wei, who was Alice Huang’s business partner and often introduced as her husband, are tied to a web of companies that connect official Nvidia partners, which can buy advanced Nvidia A.I. chips, to state- and military-linked projects.

Nvidia’s co-founder, Jensen Huang, stepped down as the company’s chief executive after acknowledging an affair with Alice Huang, who is no relation.

Companies in the Huang family’s network co-own a cybersecurity venture with an arm of China’s main military-electronics conglomerate, lease Nvidia-powered servers financed by an affiliate of its largest military aircraft maker and in one case share a parent company with a maker of radar and missile components.

Two companies that have partnerships with Nvidia, Megaspeed and Century Litong, are connected to Ms. Huang. Ms. Huang ran Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center firm that is under investigation by the Justice Department for smuggling advanced chips into China. Megaspeed has said Ms. Huang, whose involvement with Mr. Huang corresponded with a period when it was acquiring large numbers of Nvidia chips, no longer works for the company.

Ms. Huang’s family members had prominent roles and significant investments in the data center firm that founded Century Litong, which is based in Shanghai and rents out computing power to major Chinese companies and military contractors. The family members include Ms. Huang’s sister and Mr. Kang.

U.S. officials are also working to learn more about Ms. Huang and her efforts to help supply chips to data centers. The nature and extent of her ties to the P.L.A. and the companies it controls are a focus of that work, according to people briefed on the American efforts.

The ties are complex and often indirect. The research does not show whether the P.L.A. used computing power in the data centers that the family’s companies helped build. But it shows how deeply Ms. Huang and her family are intertwined with the Chinese state, and the inextricable connections between China’s tech industry and its military.

“Beijing has spent years building these networks that reach deep into Western economies,” said Greg Levesque, the chief executive of Strider. “Follow the money and, too often, you find the P.L.A. at the end of it.”

Mr. Levesque said China was exploiting more Western technology, capital and talent than ever before to build its defense industrial base. “This is happening on a scale we simply weren’t seeing a few years ago,” he said.

Nvidia declined to comment. Megaspeed did not respond to a request for comment. Ms. Huang could not be reached for comment.

From late last year into early this year, Century Litong appears to have been one of only a few sources able to supply Nvidia chips to China at the vast scale needed for its A.I. build-out, according to Strider.

Those chips were key to building the data centers that drive China’s A.I. development. Investigators are trying to determine how many of the chips that were used in those data centers were banned under U.S. export controls and, in essence, smuggled into the country. Companies controlled by Ms. Huang and her relatives were instrumental in supplying the chips, Strider found.

“Essentially, those entities worked around the controls to continue to meet the chip demands of the customers they already had, including at new data centers,” Mr. Levesque said.

On Thursday, the House Foreign Affairs Committee took the unusual step of releasing confidential information on Nvidia’s license applications to legally sell H200 chips to Chinese firms. The list showed that Nvidia had sought permission to sell more than 40,000 H200s to the Hong Kong subsidiary of Century Litong.

An Nvidia spokesman said that, despite receiving some licenses, it had already stopped shipping H200s to China, and Nvidia had not and would not ship to that firm.

Century Litong has said it has no business dealings with Ms. Huang. But the company was founded in 2023 by Century Longteng, a data center operator that was then 27 percent owned by an investment firm controlled by Ms. Huang’s sister. Mr. Kang, Ms. Huang’s presumed husband, had been Century Longteng’s executive director since February 2022, according to Strider.

In 2023, Jiangsu Lettall Electronic, a Shanghai-listed maker of metal parts for flat-screen TVs, bought 90 percent of Century Litong, and owned all of it by 2024. Lettall also owns 80 percent of Nanjing Jinning Microwave, a maker of components that Lettall has said are used in Chinese radar and missile systems. Strider said Jinning’s parts go into the P.L.A.’s DF-series missiles, including intercontinental ballistic missiles and anti-ship “carrier killers,” as well as the J-20 stealth fighter plane.

China’s defense industry wants advanced A.I. chips to design better missiles and build other military software, experts have said.

Lettall did not respond to an emailed request for comment. Asked about Ms. Huang’s network of companies and their efforts to acquire chips, the spokesman for the Chinese Embassy in Washington said he was not familiar with the situation. “We have made clear more than once our principled position on U.S. chip exports to China,” said the spokesman, Liu Chang.

Century Litong delivered servers containing Nvidia’s H800 chips to a supercomputing center in Shanghai in October 2023, according to Strider. It is unclear where Century Litong obtained those chips, but they may have been obtained legally, since U.S. restrictions on the sale of the H800 to China did not go into effect until that same month.

Century Litong now runs servers at the Shanghai supercomputing center under a lease of about $54 million from a leasing arm of the Aviation Industry Corporation of China, China’s state aerospace and defense conglomerate.

Century Litong’s reach extends far beyond the Chinese A.I. giant Tencent. When Lettall bought into the company in 2023, it said all of Century Litong’s computing business would be housed in two places: the Tencent center in Shanghai and a data center in Shenzhen.

The Shenzhen center was built for the cloud unit of Huawei, the Chinese telecom giant that has long been under sanctions by the United States over national security concerns. Huawei awarded the project in 2022 to a company controlled by Century Longteng, according to corporate filings.

Century Litong’s customers have also included a unit of China Electronics Technology Group, or C.E.T.C., a state-owned military electronics maker. The United States has included C.E.T.C. on its list of companies that it publicly identifies as doing work with the Chinese military, banning the firm from doing work with Pentagon suppliers.

Another Century Litong partner is Hangjin Technology, a listed company whose subsidiaries make chips for China’s military.

Until last December, Hangjin controlled Chaoqing, an Nvidia partner whose website once listed High-Flyer, the hedge fund behind the Chinese A.I. start-up DeepSeek, as a partner. Others on the list included the military-linked Zhejiang Lab and its co-founder, Alibaba.

DeepSeek has attracted attention for its cutting-edge A.I. models. But lawmakers in the United States have also accused it of presenting national security risks, and the federal government has banned employees from using it. The Information earlier reported ties between Ms. Huang’s network and DeepSeek.

Hangjin did not respond to an emailed request for comment. It has said it does no business with DeepSeek.

item.title: Democrats Strengthen the Legal Line with Attorneys General Triumphs
item.description:
With The Associated Press’s late declaration on Friday that a Democrat has won the attorney general’s race in Ohio, the party wrapped up a midterm election surge that will fortify the Democrats’ legal bulwark against President Trump.

Democrats ousted two incumbents and won three additional attorney general posts that had previously been held by Republicans.

Among the incumbents defeated was Kansas’ Kris Kobach, known for writing and pushing divisive state level legislation on immigration, voting and abortion restrictions. Beyond Kansas, Democratic attorneys general have taken open posts in Iowa, Texas, Georgia and Ohio, all of which are currently Republican.

Additionally, vulnerable Democratic incumbents such as Keith Ellison in Minnesota and Kris Mayes in Arizona cruised to re-election, despite Republican hopes that local concerns would overcome the national environment. Democratic newcomers easily prevailed in open contests in Michigan and Nevada as well.

With Democrats now poised to be the top law enforcement official in 29 states, they will have even more collective muscle to spearhead their party’s efforts over the last two years of the Trump administration. In the first two, Democratic attorneys general filed more than 150 cases against the administration on issues ranging from the withholding of federal funds to tariffs and the deployment of National Guard troops.

“At a time when people are worried about the rising cost of living and their rights and freedoms being put at risk, voters see that it’s Democratic A.G.s who rise to the challenge and will fight to protect them,” Sean Rankin, president of the Democratic Attorneys General Association, said in a statement.

During the campaign, Republican candidates tried to sidestep questions regarding their views on state lawsuits against the Trump administration — or on Mr. Trump, whose approval ratings have sagged in Republican and Democratic states alike. Instead, they stressed local issues, such as a social services fraud scandal in Minnesota.

But Mr. Ellison won by more than 8 percentage points over Ron Schutz, a longtime trial lawyer and Republican activist. Other triumphant Democratic incumbents in battleground states included Josh Kaul in Wisconsin and Ms. Mayes in Arizona, who won by 280 votes in 2022 but more than 10 percentage points on Tuesday.

Republicans had been bullish about Michigan, where a high-profile U.S. Senate race and control of the State Legislature were also on the line. But Eli Savit, a progressive Democratic prosecutor, defeated Doug Lloyd, a Republican prosecutor, by almost 8 percentage points — the same winning margin for Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat.

In Georgia, State Representative Tanya Miller, a Democrat and former prosecutor, won by double digits. In Texas, State Senator Nathan Johnson won comfortably as well, though by a smaller winning margin than Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa and Senator-elect James Talarico. Mr. Johnson will succeed Ken Paxton, the scandal-scarred attorney general of Texas who tried and failed to leap to the U.S. Senate.

“After years of A.G.s who mired the office in corruption and petty politics, today Texans said enough is enough,” Lottie Ash, political director of the Democrats’ attorney general group, said on election night.

In Kansas, Mr. Kobach, a longtime Republican lightning rod, lost to Chris Mann, a former police officer and prosecutor, by one percentage point, part of an unlikely Democratic surge in the state that saw State Senator Cindy Holscher win her race to succeed a Democratic governor and Adam Hamilton, a Methodist minister in Kansas, handily beat Senator Roger Marshall.

In Iowa, Attorney General Brenna Bird lost by about two percentage points to Nate Willems, a former state representative. She outperformed Representative Ashley Hinson, who lost to State Representative Josh Turek in the U.S. Senate race, and Zach Lahn, a businessman, who was trounced by Rob Sand, the state auditor, in the governor’s race.

Republicans had better news in Florida, up and down the ticket. Attorney General James Uthmeier edged Jose Javier Rodriguez, a former state legislator, overcoming a late $5 million investment by the Democratic Attorneys General Association.

And in South Carolina, where Dr. Annie Andrews, a Democrat, stunned Senator Darline Graham, David Stumbo, a conservative prosecutor, won an open race to run the office which will handle the retrial of Alex Murdaugh.

Still, Adam Piper, the executive director of the Republican Attorneys General Association, wrote in a memo that Tuesday’s results constituted “a category-five political hurricane” up and down the ballot.

Democrats won every statewide office in Texas and Georgia, and nearly did the same in Ohio. Moreover, Democrats scored new trifectas — controlling both legislative chambers and the governor’s office — in Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin — en route to netting at least 460 legislative seats.

“With an emboldened Democrat Congress, Republican A.G.s are both America’s front line and its last line of defense when it comes to their left-wing wish list — such as court packing, the Green New Deal, Medicare for All, Second Amendment restrictions, and abolishing ICE,” Mr. Piper wrote.

item.title: Preppers Are Cashing In on Tech Anxiety
item.description:
Derrick James put in his notice at work this month.

After years working for the state of Maine, Mr. James, 52, decided the time was right to go all in on his side hustle: teaching people on the internet how to survive catastrophe. Derrick James is his online identity; he asked that his real name not be used because of concerns about revealing the location of his survival preparations in the event of a disaster.

Since 2007, he has published books on topics like defending your home, posted videos about water storage and nuclear fallout, and shared recommendations on pocketknives and camp stoves. But these days especially, there is no shortage of customers.

“I’m quitting my day job for a reason,” Mr. James said with a laugh, adding that his rates for creating a single video can start around $500. He stressed that he had been thinking about leaving for some time and added that his children getting older was another factor.

Perhaps it’s the breakdown in the nation’s aviation network, or the Microsoft outage that disrupted businesses worldwide. Or the system glitches at banks, the Apple tech failures or the malfunctioning of the National Security Agency’s internal communications. Many Americans have become nervous enough to seek the help of preppers, who are more than willing to offer counsel — and cash in while they’re at it.

There is definitely something in the water right now, Mr. James and others online say. And he can sell you a straw to filter it.

Mark Lawley, a retired law enforcement officer in North Alabama, runs a prepping Facebook group with over 100,000 members. Last year, Mr. Lawley, 69, said the group gained about 30 new members per week. This fall, that number has jumped as high as 500 people, he said.

“We don’t do bunkers. We don’t do zombies. We don’t do alien invasions,” Mr. Lawley said. “We do the things that normal people are affected by, like hurricanes and tornadoes.”

With decades of experience hunting and fishing in a culture of self-reliance in Maine, Mr. James is ready to meet the moment, but he stressed that he endorses only products he truly stands behind. He is trying to balance capitalizing on the prepping boom with not trafficking in alarmism, while protecting his identity.

Preppers are preternaturally private people, Mr. James explained. Like those who follow the rules of “Fight Club,” they can be reluctant to discuss their craft, lest they lead others to their repositories during an emergency.

Others online, however, appear to be newly dipping their toes into the prepper revenue stream.

Take a cursory scroll through TikTok and you will find plenty of users talking up battery power banks and solar lanterns. A closer inspection, however, shows many sellers have no background in emergency preparedness but do see opportunities to bump up sales.

Stacie Didomenico, 39, works in long-term care but has a TikTok account with a scant following where she regularly posts products for sale with affiliate links that give her a small cut of the profits. Usually, she’s hawking fashion and household goods.

In a typical month, Ms. Didomenico, who lives in Beacon, N.Y., said she sees a few thousand dollars in sales. Since she began peddling a portable emergency radio at the end of October, that number has jumped significantly, she said.

Victoria Still, a 39-year-old stay-at-home mother of two, saw similar success selling a combo radio-flashlight on TikTok. This week, she sold just over 200 of the tools, which she said she keeps on hand for tornadoes and other unpredictable weather in Oklahoma City. That was more than double her usual sales numbers, said Ms. Still, who has just a few thousand followers.

Liz Doncaster, a prepper content creator who lives in South Florida and focuses on practical advice for people who live alone in cities, said she was somewhat frustrated by the new influx of such creators, who she felt were “trend followers.”

A retired teacher and administrator, Ms. Doncaster, 61, said she became interested in emergency preparedness after running drills at the school where she worked. Now, she has over 100,000 followers on Instagram. She has previously been accused by some online of fear mongering, Ms. Doncaster said. In the past few weeks, that tune has changed.

She said she recently charged $10,000 for a product brand deal that required her to post nine videos over three months. During the last three weeks, her inbox has been “bombarded” by potential new business, Ms. Doncaster added.

Krystal Christensen, a content creator in Utah better known online as the Doomsday Queen, launched a webinar this week charging $15 to take a “Prepping 101” class and learn basics like how to stock an emergency pantry.

Given the increased interest in prepping, Ms. Christensen, 38, said she was committing extra time to teaching others how to ready themselves.

“We’ve set aside hours out of the day so that I can help as many people as possible,” she said.

However, she was also preoccupied with securing her own supplies, adding, “We are in overdrive prepping here.”

Kirsten Noyes contributed research.
